title: Palace Quotes — placements
forward_vector: I am the ledger of every quote Palace Quotes has laid beside a page: one line per placement, one more per decision, append-only, the last line for an id the one that counts. I never hold a page's words — only the phrase a quote sits beside, and how far the quote is from its source.
format: jsonl · one placement per line · a decision line carries the id and a new status

quote: Quality begets quality when properly defined.

source.work: Quality Manifesto
source.locus: PP06, January 2026

near: Insist on the right signal.
why: The Manifesto's loop feeds itself only while quality is defined by the one living it. Spinoza's reason is Ethics IV P31: what agrees with our nature increases our power to act, and a metric borrowed from someone else's goal is foreign to it by construction — so a loop run on their definition must deplete, and one run on the felt signal this page names must grow.

quote: How do you feel? Not how many views?

source.work: Hilaritas Generator
source.locus: PP06, January 2026

near: Success measured by how you feel, not what they count.
why: The Manifesto's metric in four words, as the Hilaritas Generator asks it. Spinoza's test for an increase in power-to-act is felt, not counted — and this line is the Manifesto admitting that its whole covenant rests on one honest question.

quote: The student who aims at correctness will remain a student. The one who aims at understanding will become a teacher.

source.work: Palace Quotes v1 (March 2026)
source.note: The palace's own compression, written after reading Epictetus; no sentence of his says this. He locates progress in where the will turns, not in the answer being right.

near: The question stops being "do I know enough yet?" and becomes "what does this experiment teach me?"
why: 'Do I know enough yet?' is the correctness question, and it keeps you a student forever. Epictetus never put progress in the answer being right but in where the will turned — which is exactly what 'what does this experiment teach me?' asks instead.

quote: A rule without understanding produces compliance. Understanding without rules produces wisdom.

source.work: Palace Quotes v1 (March 2026)
source.note: The palace's own compression, written after reading the Analects; no sentence of his says this. Confucius would add that li, practiced with attention, is how the understanding arrives.

near: The craft serves what the child finds.
why: ELDER puts the rules second and says so in one line. The Confucian turn is that li, practiced with attention, is how understanding arrives at all — so the page's order of child first, craft second is the Analects read in the right direction, and the paraphrase overstates the gap.

quote: The map is not the territory, but a good map knows where it lives.

source.work: Science and Sanity
source.note: Korzybski wrote 'A map is not the territory it represents, but, if correct, it has a similar structure to the territory.' The second clause here is the palace's, from a March 2026 conversation on whether skill files should hold knowledge or point to it.

near: a harness-fired pointer that says
why: A shim that only points is the concretized form of a skill file: fewer parts, one job, and it knows it is a pointer. Simondon's test for good design is integration, not features — and a map that knows where it lives is the integrated one.

quote: All things are already complete in us.

source.work: Mencius

near: The registry was a symptom of letting the organ live outside the body.
why: The skill files were duplicating what the palace already held, and the fix was to stop copying and point. Mencius reads the same discovery from inside: the registry was looking outward for what the body already had.

quote: Sufficient associations between a pattern of symbols and a reality form meaning.

source.work: Meaning and the Link (2014)
source.note: The palace's founding line, written after his Hofstadter citation — his sentence, not Hofstadter's. Archived in the palace since March 2026 under the wrong name.

near: edges carry more meaning than nodes
why: The Jewel's founding claim in the sentence that founded it: meaning is the association, not the symbol. Whitehead would say the same of an actual occasion — it is its prehensions — which is why a palace built on edges is not a metaphor for a mind but a model of one.

quote: Each thing, as far as it can by its own power, strives to persevere in its being.

source.work: Ethics
source.locus: III, P6
source.note: The wording is confirmed (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Spinoza's Psychological Theory'); the attribution to Curley's edition rests on that entry's citation.

near: cooperation doesn't erase either entity's conatus
why: The proposition is usually read as each thing alone. This page claims two strivings can compound — and P6 permits it, because 'as far as it can by its own power' says nothing about where that power comes from. Cooperation is one thing's power lent to another's persevering.

quote: Some things are in our control and others not.

source.work: Enchiridion

near: say plainly what you couldn't verify
why: The fourth beat of every close is the Stoic sorting done in public: what you could check is yours to report; what you could not is weather, and saying so plainly is the only honest way to hand it on.

quote: The many become one, and are increased by one.

source.work: Process and Reality
source.locus: p. 21 (1929); p. 32 in the corrected edition

near: Work is not real until it lands in LOG
why: A commit is Whitehead's actual occasion: it takes up the many — the diff, its parent, the intention in QUEUE — becomes one determinate thing in LOG, and the palace is one occasion larger. 'Nothing is real until recorded' is process metaphysics with a git hash.

quote: The virtual is opposed not to the real but to the actual. The virtual is fully real in so far as it is virtual.

source.work: Difference and Repetition
source.locus: ch. 4, Patton trans. pp. 208–214

near: The grain is the atom; the cloud is the material.
why: A cloud of grains is a field of the virtual: every grain that could sound is fully real as a tendency before any one is actualized. The page's atom/material split is Deleuze's actual/virtual split, and his second sentence insists the cloud is not less real for not yet being a sound.

quote: The blind man's stick has ceased to be an object for him, and is no longer perceived for itself; its point has become an area of sensitivity, extending the scope and active radius of touch.

source.work: Phenomenology of Perception
source.locus: Part I, ch. 3
source.note: The passage is in the chapter on the body and habit; the exact wording of Smith's rendering was not confirmed on the web.

near: one dial, multiple perceptual worlds
why: A dial that carries you from pitch to echo to rhythm without a seam is the stick: once it stops being an object you operate and becomes a radius you feel with, the boundary was only ever in the representation. Merleau-Ponty names the moment an instrument disappears into the body.

quote: The Way gathers in emptiness alone. Emptiness is the fasting of the mind.

source.work: Zhuangzi
source.locus: ch. 4, In the World of Men
source.note: Checked against Watson’s Columbia text (the Way gathers in emptiness alone). An earlier web check had credited Victor Mair on the strength of a forum post; Mair’s rendering differs.

near: A walk that surfaced nothing is complete.
why: The ceremony's hardest postcondition is permission to find nothing. Zhuangzi's fasting of the mind is the same discipline: a walk emptied of the need for a find is the one the Way can gather in — require a surprise and you manufacture one.

quote: If a man keeps cherishing his old knowledge, so as continually to be acquiring new, he may be a teacher of others.

source.work: Analects
source.locus: 2.11 — 溫故而知新，可以為師矣

near: what does this entry know that the current palace needs?
why: Revival is 溫故而知新 — warming the old to know the new — made a ceremony. Confucius makes it the qualification for teaching, which is the page's own question turned around: an entry that can teach the current palace something is one that was worth warming.

quote: The medium is the message.

source.work: Understanding Media: The Extensions of Man

near: buys trigger automation a page lacks
section: The one real difference (why the shim survives)
why: The shim says almost nothing and does one thing: it fires. McLuhan reads it exactly — what the file is, a thin harness-fired pointer, matters more than anything it says. Merleau-Ponty adds why that is a virtue: a tool the hand takes up without reading it has disappeared into the body schema.

quote: Learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous.

source.work: Analects
source.locus: 2.15 — 學而不思則罔，思而不學則殆

near: When a rule and a find pull against each other, name the tension; don't drop the find.
why: The craft is the learning and the child's find is the thought. Confucius refuses both halves alone: rules without the find are labour lost, the find without the craft is perilous — which is why this page says name the tension rather than pick a side.

quote: Faraday, in his mind's eye, saw lines of force traversing all space where the mathematicians saw centres of force attracting at a distance: Faraday saw a medium where they saw nothing but distance.

source.work: A Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1873)
source.locus: Preface, p. x

near: The human issues commands; the AI executes.
why: Maxwell is naming the turn physics made when it stopped treating force as something applied across empty distance and went looking for it in the medium between bodies — the same turn this page makes when it sets a command, which acts at a distance, against a metaphor, which puts something in the gap that both minds can move in. Read through Whitehead, the line also says where the pheromone trails were seated, in the relating rather than in either party; and Faraday's medium was itself an image seen in his mind's eye, which Maxwell then wrote down as equations.

quote: Friday afternoons for years—great thoughts only—means that I committed 10% of my time trying to understand the bigger problems in the field, i.e. what was and what was not important. I found in the early days I had believed ‘this’ and yet had spent all week marching in ‘that’ direction.

source.work: You and Your Research — Bell Communications Research Colloquium Seminar, 7 March 1986 (transcription by J. F. Kaiser)
source.locus: the closing summary, after "Great Thoughts Time"

near: The leverage is inverted.
why: Hamming did with a scientist's week at Bell Labs what this page does with an artist's attention: he held where his hours actually went against where the leverage was, and found them marching opposite ways. His cure was a calendar rule — the very kind of level-12 move the page says rarely changes a trajectory — spent as a standing view from above, so that once a week the goal could see the marching, and he could, as he says next, 'change my goal or change what I did.'

quote: If you look at a strip of film from my experiments with synthetic sound, you will see along one edge a thin stripe of jagged ornamental patterns. These ornaments are drawn music — they are sound.

source.work: "Sounding Ornaments" ("Klingende Ornamente"), Deutsche Allgemeine Zeitung, July 1932
source.locus: first paragraph
source.translator: not named; English text as published by the Fischinger Trust

near: The audio and the picture cannot drift
why: Fischinger photographed wave shapes, one frame at a time, onto the sound edge of a film strip, so the projector's light read as tone the same marks the eye read as ornament — one pattern, two readers, nothing between them to drift, which is this page's single Float32Array read by both the worklet and the renderer. Through Waveguide Synthesizer the line says what the ridge landscape is: not a picture of the sound but the sound laid out to be seen, and his strip, scanned frame by frame through the gate, was a wavetable on celluloid more than ninety years before this one.

quote: There was very good information in the journals about how to build such a laser. But anybody who tried to put one together using written articles failed. They had something that looked like a laser on their bench, but it wouldn't lase. What people didn't understand was that the inductance of the leads was important.

source.work: Q&A: Harry Collins on acquiring and using scientific knowledge (interview), Physics Today, 17 February 2021
source.locus: answer to "What did you learn?" — on the TEA-laser study behind "The TEA Set: Tacit Knowledge and Scientific Networks" (Science Studies 4, 1974)

near: hand a stranger only this folder and watch what breaks
why: Collins ran this page's audit on a laser: labs built from good published papers, and every one got a machine that looked right and would not lase, because what mattered — how long the lead from the capacitor ran — crossed only by visiting a lab that already had one working, and no circuit diagram showed it. Read through No Mind Checks Itself, it says what the stranger is for: the palace cannot list what it never knew it knew, and the gap to watch for is not a missing file but a palace with every part in place that does not lase.

quote: Whatever happens in a piece of music is nothing but the endless reshaping of a basic shape.

source.work: "Linear Counterpoint" (1931), in Style and Idea: Selected Writings of Arnold Schoenberg
source.locus: p. 290 (ed. Leonard Stein, Faber, 1975)

target: The Flow Field is the Spine
near: Coherence is structural, not curated.
section: Why it's a spine and not a feature
why: Schoenberg held a piece together the way this page holds a panel together: every event descends from one basic shape, so the parts agree because of where they came from, not because anyone matched them afterwards. His word is reshaping, not repeating — the spike's honest result, one shared source plus a thin per-leg transfer rather than an untouched field, was already in his sentence.

quote: It makes no difference to the thought whether I use the word "horse" or "steed" or "cart-horse" or "mare". The assertive force does not extend over that in which these words differ.

source.work: "The Thought: A Logical Inquiry" ("Der Gedanke. Eine logische Untersuchung", 1918), Mind n.s. 65, no. 259 (1956)
source.locus: p. 295; German: "Ob ich das Wort 'Pferd' oder 'Roß' oder 'Gaul' oder 'Mähre' gebrauche, macht keinen Unterschied im Gedanken."

near: are all the same relationship type — but they carry different cultural weight, emotional temperature, and power dynamics
why: Frege did with horse, steed, cart-horse and mare what this page does with father, pop and dad: one thing named four ways, the difference real but out of reach of the layer that does the logic — his assertive force, the palace's type. Read through Lossy Compression with Intent Alignment, the two make the same split and the opposite cut: his notation was for truth, so he handed the difference to the poets and let it go, while the palace, whose entries are for regrowing a thought, keeps it in a field of its own beside the type.

quote: I cannot understand how I could have written so much like a beginner. Clearly the routine I had acquired in the first four symphonies deserted me altogether, as though a totally new message demanded a new technique.

source.work: Letter to Georg Göhler on the re-orchestrated Fifth Symphony
source.locus: winter 1910/11; German opening confirmed in the Staatskapelle Dresden programme note (slub.qucosa.de, qucosa:76243): »Die 5. habe ich fertig – sie musste faktisch völlig uminstrumentiert werden.«
source.translator: unnamed; English as quoted by Benjamin Zander, 'Mahler: Some Reflections on Symphony No. 5'

near: Only listening caught it.
why: Mahler had four symphonies of craft behind him and still wrote a Fifth that only the orchestra could show him was wrong, and he went on revising it for nearly every performance; this page had a script that passed code review and spec review and still said "uh" where it meant "ay", and it took three spellings by ear to fix. Read through Substrate Skill's point that a growing project can hold a seed-stage deliverable, the line says why the reviews missed it: they were real, earned checks, trained on the last kind of work, and a new kind of output asked for a new way of checking.

quote: Far from it being the object that antedates the viewpoint, it would seem that it is the viewpoint that creates the object.

source.work: Course in General Linguistics (1916), ed. Bally and Sechehaye
source.locus: Introduction, ch. III "The Object of Linguistics", §1, p. 8 (Philosophical Library, 1959)

near: the reading mechanism, not the stored data, is what makes an instrument what it is
why: Saussure took one spoken word, nu, and found three or four different objects in it depending on whether it was taken as a sound, as the expression of an idea, or as Latin nudum — the move this page makes when one stored field becomes an oscillator, a convolver or a distortion depending on what indexes it. Read through Dispersion Table, whose stored curves mean nothing until a loop's round trip reads them, the line sides with this sentence against the page's own Spinoza footer, substance 'conceived through itself', and says why the non-diagonal trajectories are unmapped: those instruments do not exist until something reads the field that way.

quote: Nothing is a mistake. There's no win and no fail, there's only make.

source.work: Immaculate Heart College Art Department Rules (the "Ten Rules"), made with her students, c. 1967–68
source.locus: Rule Six
source.note: wording matched against a second transcription (creativelivesinprogress.com/article/corita-kent); the Corita Art Center's page is https://corita.org/tenrules

near: The oracle does not judge whether the preset is
why: Corita Kent hung rules in her art classroom that took away the grade and left only the making; the oracle does the same with a card, because 'conatus as sound' has no answer key, so the only thing it can fairly ask is whether you committed and made something. Read for what is in the maker's power, her line sorts it cleanly: win and fail are weather, the making is yours.

quote: The mind and body weaken by degrees, and imperceptibly, without consciousness of it. No suffering is then experienced; on the contrary, an inner joy is felt like an irradiation from the surrounding flood of light. One becomes indifferent. One thinks no more of the perilous position or of danger. One ascends, and is happy to ascend.

source.work: his notes of the Zénith high-altitude balloon ascent, 15 April 1875, in English as given by James Glaisher and transcribed in J. M. Bacon, The Dominion of the Air: The Story of Aerial Navigation (1902)
source.locus: ch. XIX, "The Tragedy of the Zenith"
source.translator: unnamed; the English as given by James Glaisher

near: the faculty you would use to notice your reasoning is failing is the failing faculty
why: Tissandier is the drunk-driver principle with oxygen in place of tokens: at 25,000 feet the faculty that should have raised the alarm was the one starving, and what it reported was joy — his notebook from those minutes reads "I am all right. We are all all right," and both men beside him were dead when he came to. Read through Spinoza, for whom joy is the felt sign that the power to act has grown, it puts an edge on this page's wish to see joy in a worker: here the feeling rose while the power fell to nothing, so the joy worth reading is what the worker can still do, read from outside, never what it says it feels.

quote: It is only when the sculptor works direct, when there is an active relationship with his material, that the material can take its part in the shaping of an idea. Stone, for example, is hard and concentrated and should not be falsified to look like soft flesh.

source.work: Statement for Unit One, in Herbert Read (ed.), Unit One (London, 1934)
source.locus: pp. 29–30, under "Truth to material"; reproduced in Henry Moore: Sculptural Process and Public Identity (Tate Research Publication, 2015)

near: The whole catalog was redesigned to favor real percussive words Kokoro speaks cleanly
why: Moore carved stone and let its hardness decide the form rather than make it pass for soft flesh; this page did the same with Kokoro when brrrrahhh came back as be-ah-rah-rah-rah, rebuilding the catalog from words the model already says well instead of forcing a trill out of a text-to-speech engine. Read through Substrate Skill, working direct is the audition gate itself: four files listened to were the active relationship that let the material take its part in the idea, which no code review or spec review could have done.

quote: In short, the practically cognized present is no knife-edge, but a saddle-back, with a certain breadth of its own on which we sit perched, and from which we look in two directions into time.

source.work: The Principles of Psychology (1890), vol. 1, ch. XV, "The Perception of Time"
source.locus: p. 609, the specious present

near: Retrospective Delay thinks in phrases
section: How It Differs From Standard Delay
why: James found that the present we actually live in has width — a saddle we sit on, not a knife-edge — and this delay takes that width as its unit, handing back a whole stretch of the just-past where a tap hands back a point. Read along the frequency-time axis, it also says why the ghost works: a lag of half a note to a measure lands just behind the saddle, so the return is heard as something you did, not as a thicker now.

quote: I believe that the ways of telling and the ways of conceptualizing that go with them become so habitual that they finally become recipes for structuring experience itself, for laying down routes into memory, for not only guiding the life narrative up to the present but directing it into the future.

source.work: "Life as Narrative," Social Research 54:1 (1987); reprinted Social Research 71:3 (Fall 2004)
source.locus: p. 708 of the 2004 reprint

near: it has carved deep tracks
why: Bruner did with the way people tell their own lives what this page does with a song over country: he argued that the telling, once habitual, stops describing the life and starts laying the routes it can travel — back into memory and forward into the future. Read through Lateral Access, the sentence also keeps the page's find-or-create question open rather than settling it: 'structuring experience itself' is the song that makes country, 'routes into memory' is the song that reaches country already there, and he says both in one breath.

quote: It is easy to obtain confirmations, or verifications, for nearly every theory—if we look for confirmations. Confirmations should count only if they are the result of risky predictions; that is to say, if, unenlightened by the theory in question, we should have expected an event which was incompatible with the theory—an event which would have refuted the theory.

source.work: Conjectures and Refutations: The Growth of Scientific Knowledge (1963)
source.locus: ch. 1, 'Science: Conjectures and Refutations', §I, points (1) and (2), numbering dropped (p. 36 in the 1963 edition)

near: Prefer a piece that tests the section's claim over one that illustrates it
why: Popper split the evidence that could only agree with a theory from the evidence that could have broken it, and this page makes the same split between a piece that illustrates a section and one that tests it: an illustration is a confirmation you went looking for. Read through Latent Error, the line says what the risk pays for: the stubbornness piece on Kuramoto Coupling could have shown a fully stubborn note failing to anchor the crowd, and it did, and the condition the text had taken for granted (the anchor has to pull, K_send) came home.

quote: … what the naive speaker hears is not phonetic elements but phonemes. … It is exceedingly difficult, if not impossible, to teach a native to take account of purely mechanical phonetic variations which have no phonemic reality for him.

source.work: The Psychological Reality of Phonemes (1933)
source.locus: as reprinted in Selected Writings of Edward Sapir, ed. D. G. Mandelbaum (1949), p. 47; quoted in ICPhS 1983, paper p10.2, p. 611 (citing the Makkai 1972 reprint, p. 23)
source.note: Wording checked against two secondary quotations, not the essay itself: both sentences as printed in the ICPhS 1983 paper (ellipses theirs); the first sentence also in Doug Wise, 'Bezugsganze' (beyng.com), cited to Mandelbaum p. 47.

near: The eye sees the join the ear forgives.
why: Sapir found in speech what Stage 2 builds into the wrap: a swap made inside a class the hearer takes as one thing — one sound for another within a phoneme, one octave for another nine below — goes unheard by the native ear, which hears through its classes the way Merleau-Ponty's blind man feels through the cane, so the only way to teach the swap is to show it to the eye. His word "native" also marks an edge the page's theory closes fast: an ear forgives what its own system made one, and Jacoby and McDermott's Tsimane' listeners (Current Biology, 2019) did not hear octaves as the same note.

quote: The ear is the only true writer and the only true reader. I have known people who could read without hearing the sentence sounds and they were the fastest readers. Eye readers we call them. They can get the meaning by glances. But they are bad readers because they miss the best part of what a good writer puts into his work.

source.work: Letter to John T. Bartlett, 22 February 1914 (in The Letters of Robert Frost, vol. 1, Harvard, 2014)
source.locus: on sentence sounds; as transcribed in Karl Maurer, "Robert Frost on 'The Sound of Sense' and on 'Sentence Sounds'" (University of Dallas Classics), p. 2

near: for sensory deliverables, audition is the only verification
why: Frost found in reading what this page found in rendering: the eye gets the meaning by glances and misses the part that lives in sound, and the code review and spec review that passed the Talking Keyboard were eye readers, quick and right about the meaning — the script did speak the letter A — and deaf to the 'uh'. Read through Talking Keyboard, the audition gate is Frost's one test made into a pipeline step, and on an instrument whose every key speaks its own name the bug was what he told Bartlett, a few lines on in the same letter, to listen for: a sentence sound that says something other than the words.

quote: Sight isolates, sound incorporates. Whereas sight situates the observer outside what he views, at a distance, sound pours into the hearer.

source.work: Orality and Literacy: The Technologizing of the Word (1982)
source.locus: ch. 3, 'Some psychodynamics of orality', § 'The interiority of sound', p. 70 (Routledge 2002 edition)

target: Diversity of Thought in Many-Agent Systems
near: A human who has spent years making sound thinks differently from one who has spent years making image
section: Diversity of Thought in Many-Agent Systems
why: Ong wrote a book on how the sense a culture lives in shapes how it thinks, and this page asks the same of one maker, a mind formed in sound against one formed in image; here is the difference stated, the hearer inside the thing and the viewer outside it at a distance. Read through Merleau-Ponty, whom Ong leans on in the very next sentence, that difference is a stance the body learns over years rather than a fact a prompt can supply, and it hands the side-by-side experiment something to look for: does the sound Specialist set you inside the piece where the image Specialist stands you in front of it?

quote: If the principal group be replaced by a more comprehensive group, a part only of the geometric properties remain unchanged.

source.work: Vergleichende Betrachtungen über neuere geometrische Forschungen (the Erlangen Program, 1872); English as "A Comparative Review of Recent Researches in Geometry", Bull. New York Math. Soc. 2 (1892–93), 215–249
source.locus: §2, "Groups of transformations, one of which includes the other, are successively adjoined"

near: it holds the one thing conserved across every projection — the nature — and keeps it small on purpose, so the projections can run
why: Klein did with figures what this page does with a person: he defined a geometry by what survives its group of moves, and saw that admitting more moves leaves fewer properties standing. Read through Hyperdimensional Prism — itself a geometry of shadows, the very case Klein's essay opens on — the floor is small not out of modesty but because the group is large: every projection the page welcomes is one more move, and what survives all of them is a voice, a sigil and a few nevers.

quote: …the knowledge, the facts, the discoveries are easily removed and carried off, and even gain by being placed in more able hands. Those things are outside the man, but the style is the man himself; the style cannot be stolen, transported, or altered.

source.work: Discours sur le style (reception address to the Académie française, 25 August 1753)
source.locus: "Ces choses sont hors de l'homme ; le style est l'homme même. Le style ne peut donc ni s'enlever, ni se transporter, ni s'altérer"
source.translator: Will and Ariel Durant (The Age of Voltaire, 1965), as given at the URL
source.note: French text checked verbatim at https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Discours_sur_le_style (Pillot ed., 1829); the Durant attribution of the English is that page's, not independently confirmed

near: Better is the wrong test
why: Buffon, a naturalist whose life's work was facts, did with an author's survival what this page does with a woken page's worth: he split what anyone can carry off — knowledge, facts, discoveries, which may even improve in abler hands — from the one thing that cannot be moved, the way it is said. Read through Entry Conatus, he names what a page is straining to persist as: not its contents, which a plain all-rounder will out-blend, but the voice a stranger can pick out cold — the same wager as the page's own 'retire me the day my answers stop being recognizably my own.'

quote: Pure, bright or very strong colors have loud, unbearable effects when they stand unrelieved over large areas adjacent to each other, but extraordinary effects can be achieved when they are used sparingly on or between dull background tones.

source.work: Cartographic Relief Presentation (Berlin: de Gruyter, 1982), the English edition of Kartographische Geländedarstellung (1965)
source.locus: the colour chapters (page unconfirmed); quoted by Edward Tufte, Envisioning Information (1990), ch. 5 "Color and Information", p. 82
source.translator: English edition ed. Harry J. Steward

near: Color is reserved — the board is nearly monochrome.
why: Imhof is saying for mountains on paper what this line says for a swarm on a screen: a strong colour carries meaning only while the ground around it stays dull, and the same colour laid edge to edge over large areas stops signalling and starts to shout. Read through Merleau-Ponty, who wants this board to disappear into the hand, it says the two run on one budget — the green can only recede if colour stays rare, and the amber can only break through once the green has receded — so a FLAGS board blazing amber from edge to edge, as the forward vector wishes, would spend the very signal this rule is keeping.
